analysis.one_liner: Bans credit card tricks like hidden fees, phony pre-approvals, and late-fee due-date games.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by Rep. John LaFalce and 21 Democratic cosponsors, never got a hearing or a vote and died in a House Financial Services subcommittee when the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have written a list of credit card practices into law as unfair and deceptive, including charging application fees before disclosing terms, offering "pre-approved" cards the consumer doesn't actually qualify for, advertising terms that quietly change when the card arrives, signing people up for paid credit-protection products without clear consent, setting due dates on holidays to trigger late fees, and raising interest rates for reasons unrelated to the account. It would have let state attorneys general sue card issuers to stop these practices and win refunds for residents. The House committee that received the bill never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Credit card holders, especially people with weaker credit who are targeted by fee-heavy cards. The bill attacks the mechanics by which issuers collect late fees and add-on charges: due dates placed on days the issuer can't process payments, payments held past the due date, enrollment in paid memberships without consent, and rate increases for reasons unrelated to the account. It would also require notice to anyone rejected for advertised terms, explaining why and what they actually qualify for [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Credit card holders, especially subprime borrowers

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits charging application or processing fees before required disclosures, and conditioning a card on buying memberships or credit-protection products [S3].
Prohibits misleading "pre-approved" solicitations and bait-and-switch terms that are worse than what was advertised [S3].
Prohibits enrolling cardholders in paid services or posting charges without clear consent, and bans scheduling due dates on holidays or withholding payment posting to generate late fees [S3].
Bans interest rate increases for reasons other than the cardholder's own conduct on that account, with advance notice [S3].
Authorizes state attorneys general to sue in federal court to stop violations and obtain damages or restitution for state residents [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers, which would lose revenue from late-fee-triggering practices, add-on product enrollments, and solicitation tactics the bill defines as unfair or deceptive. Indirectly, some consumers could face tighter access to credit or different pricing if issuers reprice risk they can no longer recover through fees.

drawbacks.text: The bill leaves the specific rules to Federal Reserve regulations, so the practical protections would depend entirely on how the Board defines "unfair or deceptive" within six months of enactment [S3].

Banning rate increases unrelated to account conduct and restricting fee triggers would remove risk-management tools issuers use to price borrowers with weak credit; an honest supporter should acknowledge issuers could respond by offering less credit or higher upfront rates to subprime customers.

Expanding state attorneys general enforcement adds a layer of litigation against creditors; the bill allows federal agencies to stay or remove state suits, but issuers would face parallel state actions [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets practices whose direct purpose, as the text describes them, is generating late fees and unauthorized charges from cardholders. The cost falls on issuers' fee revenue, with a real risk that low-credit-score consumers see fewer fee-harvesting card offers and possibly less credit access; on balance the consumer protections are substantial and the design gives regulators a deadline and states a way to enforce.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, sent to the House Financial Services Committee, then to its consumer credit subcommittee, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. John LaFalce introduced the bill on March 15, 2001, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services [S5].
On March 26, 2001, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit [S5].
No further action appears in the record; the bill received no hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 107th Congress ended [S5].
The bill had 21 cosponsors, all House Democrats [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers came out ahead: the fee and add-on practices the bill targeted continued, and cardholders continued to bear them. The sponsoring members gained nothing for their effort beyond the introduction itself.

for.name: 21 of 208 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsored

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its consumer credit subcommittee and never scheduled a markup, hearing, or vote on it

against.name: Credit card issuers
against.what_they_did: Opposed restrictions on card fees, add-on product sales, and rate-setting during this era; the industry's interests were protected by the bill never advancing

sides.party_line_note: All 22 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican supported it, and the Republican-controlled committee never brought it up.

industries.note: The bill outlaws revenue practices built on late-fee mechanics, unauthorized add-on enrollments, and misleading solicitations; issuer gains came directly from charges to cardholders. Its defeat left those revenue streams intact.

industries.industry: Credit protection, credit insurance, and credit-education product sellers
industries.note: The bill bars issuers from conditioning cards on buying these products and from enrolling customers without clear consent, cutting off a channel that billed cardholders for services they often didn't knowingly order.

The practices targeted — application fees before disclosures, phony pre-approvals, terms that change on arrival — were concentrated in cards marketed to people with weak credit, who would have been the main beneficiaries of the ban.
